name: SN65HVD1050DR
title: SN65HVD1050: 5 V high-speed CAN transceiver with silent mode, SOIC-8
summary: A 5 V CAN bus transceiver to ISO 11898-2 for signaling up to 1 Mbps, offered as an improved replacement for the TJA1050, with low emissions and high immunity. The S pin chooses between normal high-speed operation and a listen-only silent mode; a dominant time-out frees the bus if TXD sticks low, and VREF provides VCC/2 for split termination. Bus pins withstand –27 V to 40 V and ±200 V ISO 7637 transients, operate over –12 V to 12 V of common mode, and thermal shutdown guards the driver. It comes in an 8-pin SOIC for –40 °C to 125 °C.
key_figures: 50 mA typ dominant, 6 mA typ recessive or silent

notes: Automotive (SN65HVD1050-Q1) and Enhanced Product (SN65HVD1050-EP) versions exist as separate parts.

pins.name: TXD
pins.function: Transmit data from the CAN controller. Low drives the bus dominant; high or open leaves it recessive.

pins.name: RXD
pins.function: Received data to the CAN controller: low while the bus is dominant, high while recessive.

pins.name: VREF
pins.function: Reference output at half of VCC, for the centre tap of a split termination. Can be left open when not used.

pins.name: S
pins.function: Mode select. Low gives high-speed (normal) mode; high gives silent, receive-only mode with the driver off.

circuits.title: Typical application
circuits.description: A 5 V node. The input supply passes a series diode into a 5 V linear regulator such as the TPS76350, with a capacitor on each side of it. The regulated rail feeds both the 5 V microcontroller and the transceiver's VCC, which has its own capacitor to ground at the pin. The microcontroller drives TXD and S and reads RXD. CANH and CANL go out to the bus; an optional split termination of two resistors with a capacitor from their centre to ground can sit across them, with VREF tied to that centre.
notes: The 60 Ω values are the split-termination halves of a 120 Ω termination; R1, R2 and C5 are fitted only at a terminating node.
The lower split-termination resistor is drawn with its upper end unconnected; it joins the centre node with the upper resistor, the capacitor and VREF.

circuits.title: Standard termination
circuits.description: One resistor equal to the cable's 120 Ω characteristic impedance across CANH and CANL, at a node that ends the bus.
notes: U1's other pins are not part of this circuit.

circuits.title: Split termination
circuits.description: The 120 Ω termination split into two 60 Ω halves in series across CANH and CANL, with a capacitor from the centre to ground. It filters the bus common mode and steadies it at the start and end of each message.
notes: U1's other pins are not part of this circuit; VREF can be tied to MID.

circuits.title: Typical CAN bus
circuits.description: Four nodes on one two-wire bus, each a microcontroller or DSP with a CAN controller and its own transceiver: an SN65HVD251, this part, an SN65HVD233 and an SN65HVD257. A termination resistor sits across the pair at each end of the bus, one on the cable and one inside the last node.
notes: The other nodes' controller links, and every node's supply pins, are not part of this circuit.
RTERM is 120 Ω, the cable's characteristic impedance.

circuits.title: Driver VOD test circuit

notes: U1's VCC, GND, RXD and VREF are not part of this circuit.

operation.text: A high-speed CAN physical-layer transceiver to ISO 11898-2, sitting between a CAN protocol controller and the two bus wires at up to 1 Mbps. It is offered as an improved replacement for the TJA1050, and its parameters cross-reference to the TJA1050's.

S low (or open, per the driver table) enables both driver and receiver. TXD low drives CANH high and CANL low (dominant); TXD high or open lets both lines float to the recessive bias. The receiver turns the CANH-CANL difference into RXD, low for dominant.

S high switches the driver off and keeps the receiver running, so RXD still follows all bus traffic while the node cannot transmit; supply current is 6 mA typ, 10 mA max. Taking S low restores transmission within ten (1 µs max). Silent mode serves babbling-idiot protection, keeping a faulty node off the bus, and the selection of one of several redundant transceivers.

A falling edge on TXD starts a timer. If TXD has not risen again before t(dom) (300 µs to 700 µs at VCC 4.75 V to 5.25 V) runs out, the driver is disabled and the bus returns to recessive, freeing it for the other nodes. RXD keeps reporting the bus meanwhile. The next rising edge on TXD clears the condition. The time-out sets the lowest usable data rate (see equations); the recommended minimum signaling rate is 20 kbps.

The driver outputs switch off when the junction reaches about 190 °C. This guards against bus shorts but does not prevent damage; a part that has gone into thermal shutdown many times or for long periods should be replaced.

VREF puts out VCC/2 (0.4 VCC to 0.6 VCC for ±50 µA) through an internal 2 kΩ / 2 kΩ divider. Connected to the centre of a split termination it helps hold the bus common mode at VCC/2. Unused, it is left open.

Dominant: the bus is driven differentially (about 3.5 V on CANH and 1.5 V on CANL nominal), matching logic low on TXD and RXD. Recessive: the lines are pulled to VCC/2 through the receiver's high-value input resistors RIN and RID, matching logic high. The recessive bias is set to 0.5 × VCC, so supply noise appears on the bus common mode.

Bus pins survive –27 V to 40 V (cross-wiring, overvoltage, loss of ground) and ISO 7637 transients of –200 V to 200 V; the common-mode range in operation is –12 V to 12 V. The CAN inputs and outputs stay high impedance with low VCC and stay monotonic while the supply ramps, so power cycling does not glitch the bus.

TXD and S each enter through 4.3 kΩ with a 6 V clamp; TXD also carries an internal current source and S a 40 kΩ resistor to ground. RXD leaves through 25 Ω with a 6 V clamp. CANH and CANL each enter through 20 kΩ to a node with 10 kΩ to ground, clamped at 40 V; CANH also carries an internal current source. VREF is a 2 kΩ / 2 kΩ divider with a 40 V clamp.

ISO 11898 sets 1 Mbps, 40 m of bus, 0.3 m stubs and 30 nodes, though careful design can exceed each. The driver gives at least 1.5 V into 60 Ω (two 120 Ω terminations) and is also specified for 1.2 V minimum through a 330 Ω coupling network over –2 V to 7 V common mode. That network stands for 90 of these transceivers at their 30 kΩ minimum differential input resistance, so up to 90 nodes fit on one segment; signal loss, ground offset and imbalance may lower the practical figure. CANopen, for example, allows up to 1 km with under 64 nodes at much reduced data rate.

The bus is twisted pair (shielded or not) of 120 Ω characteristic impedance, ended at both ends by a resistor of the same value; stubs are kept short. If a node carries the termination, removing that node must not leave the bus unterminated. Split termination (two 60 Ω with a capacitor to ground) reduces emissions from common-mode steps at the start and end of messages. Size termination resistors for a fault that puts the supply across them, which drives far more current than the transceiver's own limit.
Loop delay is TXD to the bus plus the bus back to RXD. A typical TXD-to-RXD loop delay measured on a dominant-to-recessive edge is 156.5 ns.

TVS diodes on CANH and CANL are the favoured guard against ESD, burst and surge: their low capacitance lets every node carry them without lowering the data rate, and they react in picoseconds with ratings to several kilowatts.
Decouple VCC with a 100 nF ceramic capacitor placed as near the supply pin as possible; the part runs from a 5 V rail.

ESD and EFT energy spans about 3 MHz to 3 GHz, so the bus protection is laid out with high-frequency technique. On-chip ESD protection does not cover industrial EFT and surge, so a TVS (bidirectional diode or varistor) and bus filter capacitors sit at the bus connector, in line with the signal path rather than on a branch. VCC and ground planes keep inductance low; bypass and bulk capacitors sit at the VCC pin; each bypass and protection part gets at least two vias to VCC and ground. A split termination has its centre taken to ground through a capacitor, with VREF on that centre. Series resistors on the logic lines can limit current, and capacitors at the logic inputs can filter noise.

The internal pull-up and pull-down on the logic pins are weak, so a 1 kΩ to 10 kΩ external resistor is advised to hold an open pin firmly during transients. With an open-drain host on TXD, a 1 kΩ to 10 kΩ pull-up sets the recessive state. If only normal mode is used, S needs no series resistor and a pull-down to GND can take the place of its filter capacitor.
